The turning point was one client, in 2011.

People ask me what changed, and I always start with the calendar, because that is where you see it first. I used to have one diary and it fitted in my pocket. Meetings were in the morning, court was in the afternoon, and nothing ever happened on a Sunday. I did not use to think about time zones at all. Today my first message arrives at seven, from somebody in Rotterdam who has already had lunch, and my last one arrives after ten, from Singapore. The work itself is not more difficult than it used to be. The difficult part is that it never stops arriving. And here is the thing nobody warns you about: I do not miss the old caseload, and I do miss the old calendar. Those are two different feelings, and you are allowed to have both.

Thirty years ago a commodity lawyer in this country used to be a specialist in Brazilian law who occasionally saw a document from abroad. That job does not really exist any more. The contracts moved, the arbitration moved, and the language of both of them moved with them. So today the same lawyer has to keep up with three legal systems instead of one. I am not going to tell you that this is better or worse. I will tell you the part that matters for anybody thinking about starting late. The people who made that change well were almost never the youngest. They were the ones who already knew the business by heart and only had to learn the words. Learning the words is slow, but it is finite. Learning the business takes twenty years.
